catalog_quote: Although stress is not phonemic, considerable variation in the loudness of syllables is to be heard. This is predictable in terms of two stress features: (1) phrase stress and (2) syllable stress. (1) Phrase stress: [ˇ] The domain of phrase stress is the phonological phrase, (see section 2.3). One and only one phrase stress [ˇ] will occur in each phonological phrase. (i) In non-final phrases, phrase stress occurs on the penultimate syllable if the last syllable is short; on the last syllable if it is long. ... (ii) In final phrases, phrase stress occurs on the penultimate voiced syllable if the last voiced syllable is short; on the last voiced syllable if it is long. A short vowel before final juncture is frequently devoiced. (see section 2.1.2). ... (iii) Phrase stress occurring in positions other than those described above indicates contrastive emphasis on the morpheme concerned. ... (2) Syllable Stress: All syllables are said to be stressed or unstressed. Every short syllable before any juncture is unstressed. All other syllables are stressed. Some stressed syllables are, however, heard as louder [´] than others [`] in terms of the following facts: (i) Other things being equal, a long syllable is more prominent than a short syllable. ... (ii) Other things being equal, the vowel /a/ is more prominent than the vowel /i/ or /u/. The vowels /e/ and /o/ have an intermediate degree of prominence.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive. Yasuda recognises no word-level accent: the unit that carries the single main stress is the phonological phrase (a stretch bounded by final juncture /#/ or non-final juncture //, sec. 2.3). Within that phrase the main stress sits at the right edge and is weight-sensitive: on the last syllable if it is long ((C)VV, i.e. a long vowel or vowel sequence, sec. 2.4), otherwise on the penultimate syllable; in phrase-final position a devoiced final short vowel does not count. Equivalently, stress on the penultimate mora of the phrase. A word uttered alone forms a final phrase, so in citation form this yields the familiar East Polynesian 'final long vowel, else penult' pattern, but the source frames it as phrase stress, not word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yasuda's second feature, 'syllable stress' (p. 30): 'All syllables are said to be stressed or unstressed. Every short syllable before any juncture is unstressed. All other syllables are stressed.' Among stressed syllables, long syllables are more prominent than short, and /a/ more than /e o/ more than /i u/. Within a long syllable in penultimate position the first mora is louder in fast speech and the second in slow speech (pp. 30-31: tamaiti, paapooro). No word-level secondary stress is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 30 (iii): 'Phrase stress occurring in positions other than those described above indicates contrastive emphasis on the morpheme concerned' (e.g. Kua haka+turi tee ia vahine 'This woman did flirt', stress on tee). A short vowel before final juncture is frequently devoiced (sec. 2.1.2), so the final-phrase rule counts voiced syllables. Sec. 7 (p. 162) adds that the particles e, a, o seem lengthened when they carry final phrase stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is explicitly the phonological phrase (final and non-final), not the word; stress is described as predictable loudness, 'not phonemic'. Syllables: short (C)V vs long (C)VV; long vowels are analysed as VV sequences (pp. 20-21), and stress marks are placed over a whole long syllable. Data: elicited 1966-67 in Auckland from Penrhyn migrants, chief informant Mrs Maramaakura Taia (b. c. 1909); Shibata 2003 calls this variety more Rarotonganized than that of his atoll informants.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Penrhyn/Tongarevan proper (= penr1237, ISO pnh), as spoken by migrants from the atoll living at Mangere, Auckland, in 1966-67 (chief informant Mrs Maramaakura Taia); Shibata 2003 (sec. 2.2) remarks that this variety is more Rarotonganized than that of his atoll-resident informants. No separate glottocode applies.

tone.quote: In Penrhyn five vowel phonemes, ten consonant phonemes and three junctural phonemes are recognized. Vowel Phonemes: i e a o u Consonant Phonemes: P t k m n ng r v s h Junctural Phonemes: # // + Vowel length is phonemic: ii ee aa oo uu (see section 2.1.1.) [...] 2.8. Intonation Intonation is phonemically contrastive for morpheme sequences. It differentiates interrogative sentences and imperative sentences from declarative sentences. Certain types of interrogatives are distinguished from declaratives only by intonation. [...] However, the pitch patterns have not been subjected to exhaustive analysis
tone.locator: Ch. II Phonology, sec. 2.0 'Phoneme Inventory', p. 6 (not p. 8), and sec. 2.8 'Intonation', p. 32
tone.says: Exhaustive phonemic inventory = 5 vowels, 10 consonants, 3 junctural phonemes, phonemic vowel length; stress not phonemic (sec. 2.7); pitch enters only as a property of the junctures (falling pitch before #, rising/retained pitch before //) and of sentence intonation (sec. 2.8: intonation distinguishes interrogative/imperative from declarative sentences; pitch patterns not exhaustively analysed). No tonemes or word-level pitch contrasts are set up.

sources.note: Consonant and vowel inventories only (no glottal stop; long vowels with macron); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Shibata, Norio (ed.). 2003. Penrhyn-English Dictionary (ELPR Publications Series A1-005). Suita/Kyoto: Project 'Endangered Languages of the Pacific Rim', Osaka Gakuin University / Nakanishi. xiv+237 pp. — abridged introduction as republished online at penrhyn.cookislandsdictionary.com/about (Te Ipukarea / USP Cook Islands)
sources.note: Sec. 3 'Spelling and Entry Order' gives the inventory only: 5 short + 5 long vowels ('the quantity is phonemic and the macron on vowel letters marks long vowels. Syntactically lengthened vowels are also marked with a macron'), 11 consonants incl. loan /f/. Nothing on stress or accent. Sec. 2.2 says Yasuda 1968 was the only preceding study and that Yasuda's Penrhynese 'is much more Rarotonganized' than Shibata's informants'.

tone.quote: From these facts we conclude that stress in Penrhyn is closely related to changes in fundamental frequency. It is not the absolute value of the frequency, but rather its relative value within an utterance that is perceived as stress.
